title: Medicare Spending, The Physician Workforce, and Beneficiaries’ Quality of Care
research_question: Do areas with higher Medicare spending per beneficiary deliver higher-quality care to elderly patients, and does the composition of the local physician workforce (generalists versus specialists) shape both spending levels and the use of effective, evidence-based care?
data_description: The unit of observation is the U.S. state. Quality of care is measured using twenty-four indicators developed by the Medicare Quality Improvement Organization for 2000–01 (and 1998–99), based on patient discharge records covering acute myocardial infarction, breast cancer, diabetes, heart failure, pneumonia, and stroke. Medicare reimbursement per fee-for-service beneficiary, end-of-life utilization (hospital days and ICU admission in the last six months of life), and AMI discharges/mortality come from Medicare claims via the Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care, adjusted for inflation, state cost-of-living, and beneficiary age/sex/race. Patient satisfaction and HMO enrollment are from the 1992–1995 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey. Counts of specialists, general practitioners, and registered nurses come from the 2003 Area Resource File, scaled by 2000 Census population. A subset of four quality measures is observed in both 1995 and 1999.
institutional_context: Medicare, the U.S. federal health insurance program for the elderly, exhibits dramatic geographic variation in per-beneficiary spending across states without corresponding variation in measured outcomes. Documented examples include beta-blocker use within 24 hours of heart-attack admission ranging from 50 percent in Alabama to 86 percent in New Hampshire. Prior work has shown that high-spending regions deliver substantially more intensive end-of-life care—more hospital days, more ICU admissions, more specialist consultations—without improvements in survival or patient satisfaction. At the same time, low-cost, evidence-based services such as mammography, influenza vaccination, beta-blockers, and diabetic eye exams are underused and vary widely. The local supply and mix of physicians (general practitioners versus specialists) differs markedly across states, and the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 sharply curtailed home health spending. Mounting Medicare fiscal pressure makes understanding whether additional dollars buy better care a central policy concern.
